study.title: Ezekiel 43 - The glory returns, the altar is cleansed, and the worship is restored
study.overview: This chapter shows the arrival of the glory of the God of Israel to the temple, the reaffirmation of God's presence among his people and the preparation of the altar for acceptable worship. The text links holiness, repentance and worship: the temple is not only a construction, but the place where the divine presence inhabits and where the people, ashamed of their sins, again serve the Lord according to his command. The sequence culminates in the consecration of the altar for seven days and in the promise of divine acceptance on the eighth day and from then on.

outline.title: The glory of God enters the temple
outline.explanation: Ezekiel sees the glory of the God of Israel coming from the east, with the same majesty of the previous vision. The prophet falls on his face to the ground, and the Spirit leads him to the inner court, where glory fills the house. The central point is that the temple is only really temple when the glory of the LORD occupies it.

outline.title: God's presence demands holiness and shame for sin
outline.explanation: God declares that the temple is his throne and place of dwelling among Israel forever, but recalls the sins that had profaned his name. The vision is given to produce shame and repentance, in addition to teaching the form, the entrances, the exits and the statutes of the house. The sanctity of the temple is summarized in the statement that its entire contour is most holy.

outline.title: Measurements of the altar and its orientation
outline.explanation: The text accurately describes the dimensions of the altar, its base, its steps and its square shape. The orientation of the steps to the east is highlighted and suggests order and reverence in access to the altar. The detailing reinforces that the worship is regulated by God, not by human improvisation.

outline.title: Purification of the altar and restoration of sacrifice
outline.explanation: Instructions are given for the consecration of the altar through sin offerings and burnt offerings for seven days. The Levite priests descendants of Zadok are detached as servants authorized to minister. At the end, on the eighth day, the sacrifices of burnt offerings and peaceful offerings become accepted, indicating restored worship and renewed communion.

study.context: The chapter fits Ezekiel's larger view of the restored temple after the judgment and dishonor caused by idolatry. The notes provided highlight that the purpose of this vision is not only to describe a future building, but to communicate to the generation of Ezekiel a moral and spiritual message: the presence of God requires repentance, and the restoration of worship depends on the purification of idolatry. The text also echoes the pattern of the tabernacle and its consecration, showing continuity with the culture tradition of Israel.
study.theology: The main theological emphasis is the holiness of God. His glory is not decorative, but decisive: without it, the house is empty; with it the temple becomes the place of the divine throne and of the indwelling of the LORD among his people. The chapter also teaches that sin contaminates the name of God and breaks communion, so repentance and shame for evils are part of the way of restoration. Moreover, the altar must be purified before worship, indicating that access to God requires atonement. In evangelical reading, this points to the seriousness of sin and to the need for divinely provided mediation and purification. Matthew Henry's notes see the altar as the figure of Christ, but this should be understood as interpretive reading, not as an explicit statement of the verse. The chapter, at last, points out that God accepts worship when he is sanctified according to his word.

scholarViews.insight: The vision of the temple reaches its meaning only when the glory of the God of Israel returns; the emphasis is that the house needs to be occupied by the divine presence, which comes from the east with majesty and power.
The text is read as a renewal of the covenant, in which God takes possession of the house and calls the people to remember their old provocations for repentance and restoration of communion.
The measurements of the altar are understood as accurate and intentional, indicating order in the cult; the note also highlights the unit of measurement used in the description.

questions: What most draws my attention: the glory of God filling the house or the call to repentance before restoration?
In what practical ways can my life be profaning the name of the Lord, rather than honoring him as a saint?
Am I willing to receive God's command for worship and obedience, rather than treating worship as something improvised?
study.practice: This chapter calls for a concrete response of reverence, repentance and submission. Today, this can mean examining habits, motivations and sins that compete with the presence of God, abandoning what dishonors his name. He also reminds us that worship should not be molded only by personal convenience, but by the holiness of God and by his direction. In practical terms, it is worth separating time for specific confession, prayer, and obedience, asking God to purify the heart before offering any religious service. The central application is this: seek not only activities of worship, but the presence of the holy God who receives a purified people.
study.uncertainty: The chapter is highly symbolic and the notes interpret the temple and the altar in distinct theological ways; therefore, expressions such as "mystical temple" and application to Christ should be read as confessional interpretations, not as incontestable literal conclusions of the text. There is also not enough in the notes provided to state additional historical details beyond what the chapter itself and the comments say.
